articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.snippet: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
articles.snippet: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
articles.full_text:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.
Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.
Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.
But tech stocks more broadly also fell.
Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
articles.snippet: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
articles.full_text:
Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
- Published
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not in sight.
Not all countries have the funding or capacity to do this, and at some point the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
This means the summit would end with no deal and have to be suspended. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
- Published1 day ago
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas, external.
The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.
The 'worst' COP ever?
It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (Â£91bn) by 2035 - that figure has now been removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected", said one observer.

articles.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
articles.snippet: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
articles.full_text:
FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
- Published
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.
When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.
"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," the president added.
This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
articles.snippet: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
articles.full_text:
Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
- Published
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the BeltrÃ¡n Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

articles.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
articles.snippet: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
articles.full_text:
French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
- Published
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.snippet: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
articles.full_text:
Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
- Published
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attachÃ© will now be expelled.
Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.
In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.
"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."
The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.
PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.
In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.
In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars LÃ¸kke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attachÃ© must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.
He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark.
Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

articles.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
articles.snippet: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
articles.full_text:
Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
- Published
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.
"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

articles.title: Liverpool vs Manchester United: Premier League – teams, prediction, lineups
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera

articles.full_text:
Liverpool vs Manchester United: Premier League – teams, prediction, lineups
One of sport’s biggest rivalries takes centre stage as Liverpool host a Man United side in the EPL relegation zone.
Who: Liverpool vs Manchester United
What: English Premier League
When: Sunday, November 22 , at 4:30pm (16:30 GMT)
Where: Anfield in Liverpool, United Kingdom
How to follow: Al Jazeera will have full text commentary coverage of the game with build-up from 13:30 GMT
The latest rebuild of Manchester United begins at Liverpool on Sunday with Mauricio Pochettino in the hot seat – a position that some see as the impossible job.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 4Cavaliers’ Harden passes Bryant, closes on Jordan in NBA 50-point game list
- list 3 of 4Harry Kane to miss ‘a few months’ after injury as Bayern Munich draw
- list 4 of 4Why is Pochettino the favourite to replace Carrick at Manchester United?
The match at Anfield comes four days after the arrival of the Argentinian, who only oversaw his final game as United States coach on Wednesday.
The 54-year-old is tasked with ending a 13-year wait for a 21st Premier League title – only Liverpool have won the competition as many times as the Red Devils.
United sacked Michael Carrick last week with the team third from bottom in the league and suffering their worst league start for 40 years.
Pochettino is the ninth permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired with the club’s last league title in 2014 and he is the fourth in the last three years.
United’s recent pain is made worse by Liverpool’s revival in the last decade, with the Reds sitting fourth in the table and hoping to mount a challenge this season to move clear as the team with the most English top-flight titles.
What were the key takeaways from Pochettino’s Man United media conference?
Given the swift turnaround from his previous role to his new one, Pochettino’s unveiling as United manager was combined with the pre-game media briefing ahead of the Anfield trip.
Understandably, most of the questions centred on how United’s form can be reversed in the short and long-term.
“It is about building our own way here,” Pochettino said when asked what he can do differently to the other managers who have taken on the role since Ferguson’s farewell. “The past is not going to help, to think about yesterday.”
“We feel the support and we are going to work really hard to help the players to perform. That is the priority.
“It is normal when you don’t win games that the confidence starts to go down,” he said. “I think the players need to feel from us that we believe and trust in them.
“With the schedule we have ahead we have to settle on our principles. The players are intelligent, they have quality. Sometimes it is unlocking some things that didn’t appear for different reasons.”
A key figure in any rebuilding effort will be captain Bruno Fernandes, whose future has been the subject of speculation as he has yet to agree a new deal.
Pochettino revealed he had already held extensive talks with the Portugal midfielder and indicated he remained central to his plans.
“Bruno is our captain and a very important player but other players have to feel they are important from the bottom to the top,” he said.
“We spoke, I spent three hours chatting with all the players individually. It was very nice contact.”
Questions about the squad’s fitness levels have swirled around Old Trafford, but Pochettino refused to criticise what he had inherited.
“It is about proposing that idea to be brave and take it to the field,” he said.
“We cannot talk about data without context. It is easy to manipulate data but we need to be honest, sometimes they don’t show something that you can see on the field.
“We are here not to denounce things. We are here to build something with our players.”
What have Liverpool said ahead of Manchester United’s visit?
Liverpool had lost consecutive games before their 3-1 win against bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace in their last match.
The run summed up the mixed start to life at Anfield for Andoni Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer – the former Bournemouth manager admits an epic encounter awaits.
“You don’t find bigger games than this, honestly. I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be part of these games,” Iraola said.
“We have to acknowledge the importance of the game, and also a lot of ingredients, such as their new manager.
“It is important for us in lots of different ways because we want to improve our form at home and the first chance we have to do that is on Sunday.”
Iraola also admitted he fears Pochettino, whose Premier League experience was gained at Tottenham and Chelsea, will have an advantage because he does not know the Argentinian’s preferred tactics with his new club.
“We’ve faced each other. Obviously he has a lot of Premier League games that we can look at and we can look at games in the US, but they still have this small advantage,” Iraola said.
“We don’t have references to prepare because they can go different ways that we don’t actually know.
“The staff have been working with them, so they are going to arrive well prepared. We don’t have the references that we have against other teams.”
Iraola will have to adapt on the fly and the Spaniard plans to switch up his game plan if he is caught out by Pochettino’s tactics.
“Especially the beginning of the game will be important as we have to adapt to certain things and manage the situation as quick as possible,” he said.
“Every time there is a new manager you want to impress. It happens everywhere. But we have been focusing more on us, how we can improve.”
What happened the last time Liverpool played Man United?
United were 3-2 winners when the sides met in the Premier League at Old Trafford last season.

Chelsea scored six in a League Cup win against Leeds in September, but Daniel Farke’s men erased that painful result with a superb display on their return to west London.
Just 24 hours after NFL legend Tom Brady was linked with buying a minority stake in Chelsea, the seven-time Super Bowl winner might be thinking twice about his mooted investment.

Making his full debut in Alonso’s latest bid to find a stand-in for Pedro, Emmanuel Emegha fired Chelsea ahead in the 25th minute.
Yet within three minutes they gifted an equaliser to Noah Okafor, who punished static defending to lash home.

Attack on Kryvyi Rih comes as Russian missiles land in NATO member Poland and US-led peace efforts face uncertainty.
A Russian attack on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown of Kryvyi Rih has killed two people and wounded 60 others, according to local officials.
The strikes hit the central Ukrainian city on Friday night, killing a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while six children were among the injured.

About 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and businesses were damaged, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s city administration.
Vilkul said on Saturday that Russian forces launched further missiles after emergency workers arrived, hitting rescuers, medical personnel and utility crews.
Footage released by Ukraine’s emergency services appeared to show additional strikes during the rescue operation.
Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine killed two people in the southern Zaporizhia region, according to its governor.
Russian authorities also reported six deaths, including a child, from a Ukrainian attack on a residential area in Russian-controlled Luhansk, an eastern Ukrainian region.
The violence followed a separate incident on Friday in which two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in southeastern Poland, a member of NATO, the military alliance linking the United States, Canada and European countries.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident on Friday as a deliberate provocation, questioning its timing alongside military exercises involving European countries preparing for a possible post-war security mission in Ukraine.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the airspace violation on Saturday and pledged that the alliance would defend Polish territory.
The incidents have unfolded as US President Donald Trump seeks progress in negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv.
Trump said on Friday, following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China, that the Russian leader wanted to end the war diplomatically.
Zelenskyy, however, told reporters in Kyiv on Saturday that he remained less convinced than Washington that Putin was prepared to compromise.
Moscow continues to demand Ukrainian withdrawal from the entire eastern Donbas region, which Kyiv refuses to surrender.
Zelenskyy also reaffirmed Ukraine’s ambition to join NATO, while Washington has discussed offering Kyiv security guarantees resembling the alliance’s collective-defence commitments.
Such guarantees remain under discussion as negotiations continue over how to end the war and protect Ukraine from future attacks.

India’s opposition stages protests against Meta over account removals
Youth wing of Congress party issues a seven-day ‘ultimatum’ to the US technology giant, urging it to lift all restrictions.
The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party has staged protests outside Meta offices in three cities, demanding that the United States technology company restore the Instagram accounts of its leaders.
The protests took place in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram, near New Delhi, on Friday and led to clashes with police and security guards, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress on Saturday.

In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building that houses Meta’s offices and clashed with police. In Mumbai, protesters spray-painted slogans on the walls outside, and in Gurugram they held banners reading “restore Youth Congress accounts”.
The party has alleged that on November 19, Meta illegally withheld the Instagram accounts of the youth wing’s president and the party official overseeing the wing on orders from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
In a statement accompanied by videos of the protests, the Congress youth wing said, “If Meta wants to do business in India, it must respect the Indian Constitution, not surrender to arbitrary BJP government orders.”
It had also warned Meta on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the accounts were restored.
Manu Jain, who runs the group’s social media, told the Reuters news agency on Saturday that two accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of other accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government are still restricted.
The youth wing issued a seven-day “ultimatum” to the technology giant, urging it to lift all “restrictions on opposition voices, journalists and creators”.
It asked how many Indian accounts were withheld on government orders in the past six months, and how many remain blocked. It also asked Meta to explain what it called the automated blocking of posts that mention Congress leader Rahul Gandhi or criticise Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP.
On Saturday, the protesters also posted a video of workers putting up a banner in central Delhi that mocked Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, as “Mark BJPberg” – suggesting that Meta favours Modi’s party.
Meta has yet to issue a statement on the matter.
Police action and BJP response
Police registered a complaint against four Youth Congress leaders in Mumbai and detained some protesters, Dainik Jagran English reported.
Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the ruling BJP, accused the protesters of vandalising Meta’s Hyderabad office and “flaunting it on social media”.
India is Meta’s biggest market by users.
In February, the government ordered platforms to remove unlawful content within three hours of notice, down from 36 hours. The government issued nearly 195,000 blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July, the Indian Express reported.
Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025, according to its disclosures. It said most were cases in which it was “obligated to proactively restrict content” under local law.

Who is El Chapo Isidro, the alleged cartel boss arrested in Mexico?
Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges.
Mexican special forces have arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “Chapo Isidro”, who is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, Mexico’s defence ministry said.
Meza-Flores was detained along with two other men on Friday night in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa.
Recommended Stories

The arrest comes as US President Donald Trump has been pressing Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to do more to combat drug cartels and said on Friday that Washington was working with Sheinbaum “because the cartels are running Mexico.”
“I told her that,” he said. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbour.”
Who is Chapo Isidro and what is he accused of?
Despite the similar nickname, Meza-Flores is not related to Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, the jailed former leader of the Sinaloa Cartel.
Mexican authorities say Meza-Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. The Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said he was wanted in Mexico on an arrest warrant for organised crime and drug offences and is subject to an extradition order to the United States.
US prosecutors first indicted Meza-Flores in 2012. In a 2019 indictment, they accused him of conspiring to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana for the US market between 2005 and 2019. He also faces a firearms charge.
The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, and the US Department of State offered up to $5m for information leading to his arrest and conviction.
“Known as El Chapo Isidro, he’s accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs, first as an independent drug trafficker and later as the head of the Meza-Flores cartel,” said then-acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll in announcing his addition to the list.
He also said Meza-Flores and his organisation were accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture and murder.
How was Chapo Isidro arrested?
Mexico’s defence ministry said the operation followed coordination between Mexican and US intelligence agencies and involved special forces from Mexico’s National Guard and army.
Troops used “stealth and surprise” to establish a security perimeter around a house in Guasave and came under attack with gunfire and explosives before entering and arresting three men, the ministry said.
It identified the other two as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, who they identified as a financial operator. The three men were flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Sinaloa’s public security agency urged residents to stay indoors, avoid the area, and stay off the roads, as federal personnel had been attacked in Guasave.
The defence ministry said roadblocks were reported in four areas of Sinaloa after the arrests and that security forces were sent to reopen roads.
Videos from Guasave showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as cars and petrol stations on fire, The Associated Press news agency reported.
Mexico’s security secretary, Omar Garcia Harfuch, said on Saturday that troops would remain in Sinaloa to protect residents.
“These detentions are an important step toward restoring peace in Sinaloa,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: What happens between the US midterm elections and January, when Democrats take control of Congress?
articles.full_text:
US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
What happens between the US midterm elections and January, when Democrats take control of Congress?
The United States midterm elections are over, and the Democrats have won control of both houses of Congress. However, they do not take power until January.
Election officials are still certifying results, while the newly elected lawmakers are preparing to take office, and the outgoing Congress is continuing its legislative work.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Jeffries shifts strategy amid growing Democratic divisions in US House
- list 2 of 3Abdul El-Sayed’s victory is a blow to the politics of Islamophobia
- list 3 of 3How is US Senate majority leader chosen?
So what happens between now and January, and what will change as the 120th Congress takes office?
What has happened so far?
After the elections, officials have been finalising the results and completing the certification process, which varies by state.
On November 9, the existing Congress returned to Washington for what is known as the “lame-duck” session.
A lame-duck session occurs when Congress meets after an election but before the new Congress takes office.
This means the Republicans still have the majority in both chambers of Congress and can continue passing legislation until the new Congress takes office in January.
November-December: New lawmakers prepare to take office
During this time, newly elected members start preparing to take office in January.
They attend orientation sessions in Washington, hire staff, and learn more about how Congress operates day-to-day.
Political parties also choose their leaders in the House of Representatives and the Senate. The party controlling each chamber selects the majority leader, while the other party selects the minority leader. The House will also vote on a speaker, who leads the House leadership.
The Republican Party has already re-elected John Thune as its Senate leader, entering the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.
The election on the Democratic side, however, is shaping up to be more of a fight.
Among Democrats, Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Senator and current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York to be Senate majority leader, with a vote scheduled for December 1.
Speaking on Al Jazeera’s This Is America, Democratic strategist Roger Fisk suggested that the differences between the two candidates may be more about their methods than their political goals.
“I think the difference would probably come in the how rather than the what,” Fisk said.
Republican strategist Doug Heye said the leadership debate reflects wider questions facing both parties after the midterms.
“Both parties have somewhat of an identity crisis,” he said, referring to the Republicans’ losses and the future of the party but also the divisions in the Democratic Party between moderate Democrats and more progressive ones.
December 11: A government funding deadline
One of the biggest challenges of the current Congress is a December 11 deadline to approve government funding.
Congress passed a temporary spending bill, known as a continuing resolution, to keep the federal agencies functioning without approving a full-year budget.
But before the measure expires, Congress must approve another bill to keep the government funded.
If lawmakers do not reach a deal, part of the federal government could face a shutdown.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Heye suggested a temporary funding extension could push negotiations into February, by which time Democrats will control both chambers.
“So that would probably go through February,” he said, referring to a possible continuing resolution.
Heye also said the federal debt ceiling is another challenge for the new Congress.
“These are two things that never come up on the campaign trail, but it can be very important to tell us about the next two years,” he added.
December 17-18: Congress wraps up
The current Congress is expected to finalise its legislative work before the Christmas holidays.
The House’s final sitting day is planned for December 17 and the Senate’s for December 18.
But lawmakers could remain in Washington longer if major issues remain unresolved.
Even if lawmakers finish their work earlier, the 119th Congress’s term does not officially end until January 3.
January 3, 2027: The new Congress takes power
The 120th Congress starts its term at noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, 2027.
But January 3 falls on a Sunday, and Congress could pass a law setting a different date for the first meeting.
When the new House convenes, lawmakers must elect a Speaker before being sworn in. Newly elected senators will also take their oaths.
With Democrats controlling both chambers, they will gain authority over congressional committees, legislative priorities and investigations into the administration of President Donald Trump.
“You’re going to have in the House and the Senate something called committee chairs, and they’re all going to be Democrats, and they’re all going to have subpoena power,” Heye told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned that congressional investigations could complicate negotiations between Democrats and the White House.
What changes politically in January?
Trump will remain president after the midterms, but he will face a Congress controlled by Democrats in both chambers.
This means his administration will have to negotiate with the Democrats to pass legislation, while a Democrat-led Senate will control the confirmation process for presidential nominees.
Democrats will also be able to launch congressional investigations and hold hearings looking at the president’s actions and the actions of those in his inner circle and administration.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has already outlined some of the party’s priorities.
“We need to end the war of choice in Iran. We need to stop the Trump tariffs,” he said.
He also called for reversing Medicaid and food assistance cuts and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.
But Democratic control of Congress does not guarantee those policies will become law. Trump can veto legislation, while overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
“I would hope that […] each side would at least be willing to give each other 60 to 90 days to see where they might be able to cobble together a couple wins on behalf of the American people,” Fisk, the Democratic strategist, said.

articles.title: Trump, Xi agreed that military AI decisions should involve humans, Bessent says
articles.snippet: The agreement was among the major achievements of Trump's trip to Asia, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed humans should always be involved in military decisions that use artificial intelligence technologies, even as the two countries compete for AI supremacy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday.
Bessent told CNBC after returning from Trump’s meeting with Xi in Shenzhen, China, that the agreement was among the major achievements of Trump’s trip to Asia.
“I think it was very important that President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” Bessent said, referring to the Trump administration’s preferred term for the technology, “super intelligence.”
Bessent said that the U.S.-China agreement on military use of the technology, requiring human involvement and other safeguards, would not be affected by the two countries’ competition for AI supremacy. He added that U.S. AI labs needed to maintain their technological lead as the best defense against “dangerous” Chinese AI models that are being used in cyberattacks.
“But there’s nothing to do with competition when it says that both sides agree that no major military operation should be launched without a human being involved,” Bessent said.
He said that the spying allegations involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese national that he was romantically involved with did not come up in the Trump-Xi bilateral meeting.
Bessent said that Nvidia’s second-tier AI chip, the H200, remained the most advanced chip that China could purchase with licenses, after Trump took what he called a “very firm line.”
“I think what we have seen is a paucity of orders from the Chinese on the H200s as they try to build out their own chip stack, and I think that they are probably many years behind,” he added.
Bessent downplayed differences that he had voiced between the views of Treasury and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on AI chip restrictions in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, saying Trump administration officials were “all committed to following President Trump’s instructions.”
The Commerce Department took steps on Monday to further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips, including those used by overseas data centers where Chinese entities can rent computing power.
“I think we are going to see that the proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed,” he said.

articles.title: German attack drones pass live-fire tests, with first deliveries planned this year
articles.snippet: Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s military procurement office said.
articles.full_text:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s military procurement office said.
Though the systems have yet to complete qualification, the German Army plans to begin equipping its armored brigade in Lithuania in 2027.
The trials, held the week of Nov. 9, tested whether Stark’s Virtus and Helsing’s HX-2 could reliably hit designated targets and whether their warheads worked as intended on impact. The Bundeswehr conducted key parts of the testing at its weapons and ammunition test center in Meppen. The procurement office announced that both systems passed but did not disclose how many shots it fired or the weapons’ success rates.
Photos attached to the statement showed both an OWE-V Virtus and an HX-2 loitering munition moments before impact into a tank.
Both systems are loitering munitions, weapons that can remain airborne over an area while searching for targets before a human operator decides whether to authorize a strike. The live-fire campaign focused on the final part of that process, from the approach to the target through the effect of the warhead, rather than certifying the systems for service.
The military noted that before loitering munitions can be used within the German Armed Forces, they must be thoroughly tested on the “interaction of the various system components.”
German lawmakers were previously skeptical of approving armed drones for the country’s military, and some arms control researchers have raised concerns about autonomous targeting in loitering munitions.
The tests follow a Feb. 25 vote by Germany’s parliamentary budget committee approving contracts worth €268 million ($294.4 million) apiece for Stark and Helsing. Options could add €1 billion to each deal, but further purchases depend on the systems proving technologically mature and lawmakers approving the spending, Defense News reported in February. The vote marked a shift that’s part of a larger rethinking of Germany’s military posture in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Germany is trying to shorten the time between signing a contract and getting the weapons to troops by allowing concurrent development, testing, qualification and preparations for use. The procurement office said it brought soldiers into testing early so their feedback could inform changes to the systems. Lawmakers attached reporting requirements to the spending plan, and cancellation clauses allow the government to walk away if a system fails qualification.
The procurement office said it expects initial deliveries this year so troops can begin training. It did not say how many weapons would arrive in that first batch. The army intends eventually to link the munitions with its reconnaissance and strike systems, with the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania slated to become the first major formation to receive them starting in 2027.

PARIS — The Netherlands presented a defense-industrial plan with a target to grow its defense technological and industrial base by 40% by 2030, with local defense industry revenue reaching around €15 billion ($16.5 billion).
The government has earmarked €1.6 billion for the industry plan, with a focus on integrated air and missile defense, data-driven command and digital resilience, unmanned and autonomous systems; and military sustainment.
The Netherlands is the seventh-biggest defense spender among European NATO countries, ahead of Sweden, based on data from the alliance, yet the country lacks major defense prime comparable to Sweden’s Saab, Germany’s Rheinmetall or the United Kingdom’s BAE Systems.
Still, the nation of 18 million punches above its weight in several defense technology areas. For example, France’s Thales has a large part of its radar business in the Netherlands, while the country is also home to Destinus, a defense technology company which said this week its Ruta cruise missiles were used by Ukraine to target the Kerch Strait bridge.
“Through this national program, the government, together with industry and research institutions, is rolling up its sleeves to ensure that the armed forces get what they need, both now and in a conflict situation,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.
Warfighting is fundamentally changing, and the impact of technology is “enormous,” the government said, citing space technology, the electromagnetic spectrum, artificial intelligence, cyber, drones and long-range weapons. At the same time, the war in Ukraine has shown the importance of mass, production capability, stocks and the ability to sustain the fight, according to the government.
Strengthening the Dutch defense industry will strengthen the warfighting ability of the Dutch armed forces, according to the government. Spending on the plan will include €600 million for industrial ecosystems and scaling production, €320 million to help pay for international cooperation, and €150 million on make supply chains more resilient.
The Netherlands is counting on the domestic share of Dutch defense-industry revenue to grow faster than the industry’s overall revenue, climbing 50% by 2030 to more than €10 billion. Meanwhile, the target is for exports to grow by about 25%.
The MoD will give greater weight to the origin of products and suppliers in procurement decisions in 2027, and introduce procurement guidelines from the first quarter of 2028 that take into account the origin of raw materials and components, as well a supply-chain transparency, the government said.
The Netherlands is betting on international cooperation in the focus areas, and will actively contribute to leading groups for joint capability development with like-minded partners including Belgium, Germany, France, the U.K. and the Nordic countries, the government said.
“Thanks to their innovative capacity, the Dutch defense industry and research institutions are in a good position to play key roles in global value chains and in this way help reduce risky strategic dependencies for the Netherlands and Europe,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.
To improve financing access for defense firms, the Ministry of Defence together with Invest-NL will set up a €200 million investment fund for dual-use companies in defense and security.
The MoD will also set up the National Institute for Defence Technology, or NIDT, in 2028, with a budget that will climb to €350 million a year by 2030, the government said. The goal of the new institute will be to accelerate innovation and scaling up.
The government plans to strengthen protections against unwanted takeovers and investments in strategically important Dutch defense companies, as well as against leaks of sensitive technology and expertise, with a target to have additional legal instruments in place from 2028.

articles.title: US missile shortages create a range problem, report shows
articles.snippet: A new CSIS report warns that the Iran war has strained US missile stockpiles, raising concerns about America's readiness for a potential conflict with China.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. has burned through stockpiles of critical long-range missiles, which may force military forces to fall back on munitions with ranges of under 300 miles, according to an analysis this month by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The report analyzed data on munitions expenditures that were current as of November 3 to provide estimates of how missile usage against Iran is affecting U.S. defense posture globally.
“In the 39-day campaign until the April 8 ceasefire and subsequent operations, the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories,” according to the report.
It points out that, while the Pentagon has made agreements with manufacturers to boost production rates and Congress may provide funding, time is of the essence to rebuild the U.S. arsenal, as the current strain on stockpiles has created vulnerabilities.
“Does the United States have enough munitions to renew the fight? The short answer is yes—against Iran. Against China, there is great concern. Rebuilding inventories will require a multiyear commitment extending beyond the current crisis,” the analysis notes.
CSIS produced a list of missile types sorted into nine categories. Seven of the nine categories were classed as having “detrimental effects” in terms of resupply capacity.
According to this analysis, Patriot missiles, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles, and Standard Missiles, which are vertically launched surface-to-air missiles, are listed as “heavily used, no substitutes,” indicating that stockpiles are in dire condition.
Long-range ground-attack missiles including Tomahawks, AGM-158 JASSM cruise missiles, and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs) are described as being “heavily used” with “some substitutes.”
The only missile types listed as having “no significant constraints in most scenarios” are short-range munitions – including air-to-air missiles and short- and medium-range missiles, including GBU-39B small-diameter bombs and the AIM-120 AMRAAM, which is primed to strike low-altitude targets.
CSIS observes that, while the U.S. is still capable of leveraging existing missiles against targets in the short term, shortages of long-range munitions create operational challenges.
“The United States has large numbers of munitions with the same explosive yield and accuracy as the long-range systems described above but with ranges under 300 miles,” according to the report.
The U.S. is at risk of losing its ability to project power through ballistics across long distances.
At the same time, munitions with shorter ranges increase the importance of establishing air superiority. This could create complexities if the U.S. faces a powerful adversary that has sufficient air power and defenses to fend off shorter-range weapons and prevent them from being effective.
“Although production rates are increasing, demand exceeds supply—from both the United States and allies—so timelines have lengthened,” the report warns. “The problem is not money, assuming Congress continues its support, but time.”

articles.title: Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland, hoping to end conflict
articles.snippet: Denmark's parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future.
articles.full_text:
Denmark’s parliament unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland on Thursday, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island’s future that has rattled transatlantic relations.
The U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September after President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich self-governing Danish territory of 57,000 people.
“This agreement modernizes the United States-Denmark-Greenland defence partnership and bolsters the national security of the United States and our allies in NATO,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement posted on X.
The executive agreement takes effect once Denmark’s foreign ministry tells the U.S. in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete. It does not need approval from the U.S. Senate.
It expands the US military’s role in Greenland, including permission to establish a “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
The signatories will now start work on a new Greenland law to screen outside investors on security grounds and plans for two new US military bases, as outlined in the agreement, Denmark’s Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters.
“I expect that the U.S. will now also start to be more concrete on the purposes and the arrangement around these two areas,” he said.
Trump’s refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January and months of intensive negotiations.
Difficult time for Greenlanders
Naaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic member of the Danish parliament, said Trump’s pressure had led to distrust in Greenland towards the U.S. administration.
“It’s been really difficult for Greenlanders these past two years. It’s been seeping into every aspect of our lives,” Nathanielsen told Reuters. She hoped the agreement would open a path to dialogue after hurtful rhetoric within the Western alliance.
Greenland’s parliament ratified the deal this month. Danish lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalize the situation in Greenland.
Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, said the deal was more likely a beginning than an end.
“With the treaty in hand, the U.S. will be able to demand greater influence on decisions that have security policy implications and on part of the extraction of strategic resources,” he said.
Other experts say the new agreement does not add much U.S. military access to Greenland. The northernmost U.S. base is already in Greenland, which lies on the shortest route from Europe to North America.
Trump last month said that “massive oil, gas and mineral exploration” was set to begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has banned new drilling for crude. Denmark has said any resource extraction must respect local law.

articles.title: Pentagon lacks ‘overarching plan’ for munitions production, watchdog warns
articles.snippet: “DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
articles.full_text:
Facing depleted stockpiles, the Pentagon is briskly trying to ramp up manufacturing of munitions.
The problem is that it is ordering missiles, artillery shells and other munitions without regard to what the military actually needs, according to a new report.
“DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
Pentagon officials told investigators that “in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”
The GAO report is the public version of a classified study completed in September 2026. Thus, it doesn’t include “information that DOD deemed classified or sensitive, such as trends in DoD munitions inventories, persistent shortfalls and how these shortfalls have affected DOD’s support to war plans.”
Nonetheless, the report does hint at a mismatch — real and potential — between what the Pentagon is buying and what the military needs.
The Army is desperately trying to boost production of 155mm howitzer shells after
shortages were exacerbated in support of allies and partners. That effort is already plagued by manufacturing woes such as a new Texas plant that cost nearly $500 million, but failed to produce any shell components.
Now the question is exactly how many shells the Army needs.
The “Army’s ramp-up in production of 155-millimeter artillery shells to address shortages exacerbated by U.S. support to allies and partners was not driven by a need to address DoD’s total munitions requirement,” GAO said.
“DOD is taking steps to increase production in response to real shortages,” Diana Moldafsky, a director of GAO’s Defense Capabilities and Management team, told Defense News. “That said, we found some cases where DOD increased production in response to immediate shortages without basing the increase on its total requirement for that munition.”
Nor does the Pentagon have a good grasp on how much ammunition it actually has.
Each military service has its data system to track munitions inventories, which is then aggregated by DoD’s Munitions Readiness Initiative to provide, in theory, a near real-time glimpse of stockpiles as well as supply chain links.
“In total, MRI pulls from 37 DOD data sources through a mix of automated connections and some manually updated data,” GAO noted.
However, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment “does not consistently reconcile MRI munitions inventory data against the services’ own data systems.” Nor does it have “a data management plan detailing how data is aggregated in the MRI tool from across the services.”
“MRI does aggregate from the individual services’ data systems, but we found instances where the numbers in the tool differed from the services’ databases,” said Moldafsky.
Authority over munitions inventories is also fragmented among multiple offices within the DoD and the program executive offices in individual services. Working groups that are supposed to bring them together lack authority and accountability.
All of which points to the root of the problem: no one is really in charge. “DoD has not identified an office or entity and delegated to it authority that empowers the leadership to make decisions that improve munitions inventories departmentwide and hold them accountable for the outcomes achieved, such as improving munitions inventory levels,” the GAO report notes.
GAO recommended that DoD create an overarching plan to match munitions requirements, production and funding, as well as metrics to track progress. Without it, the report warns, the “DoD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement.”

articles.title: France and Sweden hold first joint nuclear-deterrence exercise
articles.snippet: The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France and Sweden held their first joint exercise under the forward deterrence initiative proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron, with French nuclear-capable Rafale jets and an Airbus A330 MRTT tanker aircraft operating over Sweden alongside Swedish Gripen fighters.
The exercise, dubbed Excalibur, was held in northern Sweden on Nov. 16 to 18, with the aim of improving interoperability between the French and Swedish air forces, the two countries’ armed forces said in statements on Thursday. The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
The French-Swedish cooperation follows an exercise last month in which British Eurofighter Typhoon jets escorted French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission. France has been working with several European allies to implement Macron’s proposal to bolster European deterrence, in the face of nuclear saber-rattling by Russia and uncertainty about United States security guarantees.
France’s nuclear deterrent consists of an ocean-based component comprising strategic ballistic-missile submarines, as well as an airborne component consisting of Rafale jets capable of carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles developed by MBDA.
“Since the in-depth dialogue on ‘forward deterrence’ was initiated, France and Sweden are taking steps to implement their common roadmap for strategic cooperation,” the Swedish Armed Forces said. The exercise “demonstrates our joint readiness and capability to act together and reflects the commitment of our two countries towards deterring threats and strengthening allied security.”
The deployment of the Rafale jets alongside Gripen fighters, with the support of an A330 MRTT, demonstrated the high level of interoperability between the two air forces in the areas of nuclear deterrence, in the service of Europe’s security, the French Armed Forces General Staff said in a post on the social network X.
“This type of deployment not only allows to test the dispersion of French aircraft to improve their capability to survive an adversary disabling strike, but also opens the door for new modes of operation previously unimaginable, such as attacking targets deep within the Russian Arctic or planning much smaller raids without needing in-flight refueling,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X.
Sweden’s Gripen fighters are “excellent combat aircraft” specifically designed to penetrate Russian ground-to-air and air-to-air defense systems, and they could be valuable assets during a nuclear strike mission, while freeing up conventional Rafale jets for other missions, Marcuz said.

articles.title: Autonomy firm Auterion to launch joint venture with Ukrainian drone maker Skyfall
articles.snippet: The new venture, called Skyfall X Auterion, will produce Skyfall drones with Auterion software in Germany, “outside the range of air strikes,” Auterion said.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — American autonomous software firm Auterion and Ukrainian drone producer Skyfall plan to form a joint venture to “manufacture drones for Ukraine at high volume in a new factory in Germany,” Auterion announced today.
The new venture, called Skyfall X Auterion, “is being established under the auspices of the official ‘Build with Ukraine’ defense cooperation framework,” the announcement said.
According to Auterion, “initial production” by the joint venture will “focus on the Shrike FPV platform” and is expected to later expand to Skyfall interceptors as well as middle- and deep-strike systems. “Every drone combines a Skyfall airframe with Auterion avionics” as well as Auterion’s operating system, the company said.
Auterion and Skyfall previously partnered for drone production for Ukraine, but Auterion said today that a German factory in particular “adds production capacity outside the range of air strikes, while maintaining a knowledge link and short innovation cycle available to Skyfall’s engineers.
“Feedback from units at the front reaches those engineers every week and goes straight into the German line,” the company said.
Auterion, which is based in Munich as well as the US, said the agreement was inked during the German-Ukrainian Economic Forum today, and Reuters reported that the German government would provide funding for the new factory and for drone orders. Citing an industry official, the newswire reported the funding would be in the range of hundreds of millions of euros first to provide drones to Ukraine and then to the German armed forces.
“SkyFall and Auterion have put more than 50,000 drones into the hands of Ukrainian units with advanced terminal guidance and target detection” Lorenz Meier, founder and CEO of Auterion, said in the announcement. “A factory in Germany gives German forces a domestic source for the same drones Ukrainian units rely on every week.”
